summary: Decide whether an integer reads the same forwards and backwards (negatives are never palindromes).
mainInsight: Extract digits with % 10 and // 10 instead of converting to a string; reversing the digits (or only the second half) and comparing is O(log n) time and O(1) space.

approaches.name: Convert to string
weaknesses: Uses extra string memory (often disallowed as a follow-up)

approaches.name: Reverse the whole number
approaches.summary: Build the reversed integer digit by digit and compare with the original.

approaches.name: Reverse only half the digits
approaches.summary: Stop when the reversed half >= the remaining half, then compare (handle odd length by //10).
weaknesses: Fiddlier for odd length and trailing zeros

personalSolution.notes: Correct and optimal asymptotically. Half-reversal is the common follow-up (and avoids overflow in fixed-width languages).

promptVariants: Which technique solves this problem, and what in the statement or constraints points to it?
Name the technique you would use here and the clue in the problem that tells you.
What approach fits this problem, and which part of the statement gives it away?
cards.answer: Reverse half of the number with % 10 and // 10 and compare it with the other half. Clue: A palindrome reads the same reversed, digits can be peeled off with remainder and integer division, and negative numbers can never qualify, so compare the number with its reversed half.
keyPoints: A palindrome reads the same reversed, digits can be peeled off with remainder and integer division, and negative numbers can never qualify, so compare the number with its reversed half.
cards.explanation: Reversing only half stops the loop in the middle and avoids overflow, and an odd length is handled by dropping the middle digit.

rubric.technique: Reverse half of the number with % 10 and // 10 and compare it with the other half

alsoValid.name: Convert to a string and compare it with its reverse
alsoValid.note: works, but uses extra space and skips the digit arithmetic

rubric.clue: A palindrome reads the same reversed, digits can be peeled off with remainder and integer division, and negative numbers can never qualify, so compare the number with its reversed half.

promptVariants: How do you test a palindrome integer without converting it to a string?
Which digit-manipulation technique solves Palindrome Number in O(1) space?
options: Peel digits with % 10 and // 10 to build the reverse
Binary search on the value and compare digit sums
Hash set of the digits seen so far in the number
Sort the digits and compare to the original order
cards.answer: Peel digits with % 10 and // 10 to build the reverse
cards.explanation: x % 10 gives the last digit and x // 10 drops it, so you can rebuild the reversed number arithmetically.

incorrectOptionExplanations.Sort the digits and compare to the origi: Sorting destroys the order you need to compare.

promptVariants: Why is it enough to reverse only half of the number?
cards.answer: A palindrome's second half mirrors the first. Reverse digits from the end until the reversed part is >= the remaining prefix, then compare (dropping the middle digit for odd length). This halves the work and avoids overflow.
cards.explanation: You never need the full reverse.

promptVariants: Which inputs are rejected up front or need special care?
Which edge case do negative numbers and trailing zeros illustrate?
options: Negatives and non-zero multiples of 10 are never palindromes
Only negatives need special care; trailing zeros are fine
Zero is not a palindrome, so it must be rejected up front
Numbers above 2^31 only, since they overflow the reverse
cards.answer: Negatives and non-zero multiples of 10 are never palindromes
cards.explanation: '-121' reads '121-' backwards; 10 reverses to 01 = 1, which is not 10 (the full-reverse approach handles it naturally, the half-reverse approach needs an explicit check).

incorrectOptionExplanations.Only negatives need special care; traili: Trailing-zero numbers are another trap for half-reversal.

promptVariants: Reversing the digits of x takes ___ time in terms of the value x.
cards.explanation: One iteration per decimal digit, and the digit count is about log10(x).

promptVariants: What is the space complexity of your solution, and why is that a benefit over str(x)?
Why does reversing digits arithmetically beat converting to a string in terms of memory?
cards.answer: O(1): only a few integer variables. The string approach allocates O(d) characters.
cards.explanation: The 'without converting to string' follow-up targets exactly this.

promptVariants: Walk through why `reversed_x = reversed_x * 10 + last_digit` rebuilds the reverse.
What do the three lines in the loop do to `tmp` and `reversed_x`?
cards.code:
while tmp > 0:
    last_digit = tmp % 10
    reversed_x = reversed_x * 10 + last_digit
    tmp //= 10
cards.answer: Each iteration moves the last digit of tmp onto the end of reversed_x: multiplying by 10 shifts existing digits left, adding last_digit appends it, and tmp //= 10 discards that digit. After all digits are consumed reversed_x is x written backwards.
